The reproductive biology of Atlantic wolffish begins with the deposition of demersal eggs, each measuring approximately 3.9 cm [Lb = approximately 3.9 cm] in diameter. These large, yolk-laden eggs are among the largest recorded for any teleost fish found in the North Atlantic, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes offspring size over fecundity. Following fertilisation, the embryonated eggs are actively guarded by the male parent during an extended incubation period. When maintained at a stable temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the embryos require a total of 174 days [ab = 174 days] to complete development before eclosion occurs. This protracted incubation period is consistent with the cold, stenothermal conditions of their deep-water habitat. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larvae are relatively large and well-provisioned, allowing them to sustain a lecithotrophic existence for several weeks before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The considerable investment in egg size and incubation duration is an adaptation that enhances larval survival in the food-limited benthic environment where these fish establish themselves after settlement.

As the yolk-sac larva develops and begins exogenous feeding, the pelagic larval phase gives way to a benthic juvenile stage. Juveniles grow steadily over several years, gradually increasing in total length. Longitudinal field studies have indicated that the transition to sexual maturity, characterized by the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, occurs when individuals reach a total length of 47 cm [Lp = 47 cm]. This length at puberty represents a critical milestone in the life history, as it marks the point at which energy is first directed toward reproductive tissue development. The time required to achieve this length at a water temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C] is substantial, with hatched individuals reaching this size after approximately 6.8 years since hatching [tR = approximately 6.8 years since hatching] in the wild. This delayed maturation is typical of a slow-growing, long-lived species inhabiting a resource-poor environment. The corresponding age at first reproduction is thus deferred until the fish have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of spawning and nest guarding.

Once the reproductive threshold is attained, females produce a single clutch of large eggs annually. At the reference length of 125 cm and a water temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], a gravid female produces approximately 34.9 offspring per day . This daily production rate, resulting in a total annual clutch of several thousand eggs, is surprisingly modest for a fish of such large body dimensions when compared to the fecundity of many other marine teleosts. The trade-off between egg size and fecundity is evident, as each 3.9 cm [Lb = 3.9 cm] egg represents a significant maternal investment. The reproductive output is constrained by the available space within the body cavity and the high energetic cost of producing such large, yolk-rich oocytes. Consequently, the annual reproductive effort is limited, and females are thought to spawn only once per year, a pattern consistent with the species' low natural mortality and extended lifespan.

Adult Atlantic wolffish are known for their considerable ultimate size, with individuals commonly attaining a total length of 150 cm [Li = 150 cm] in the wild. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of the largest individuals reaches approximately 18000 grams [Wwi = approximately 18000 grams], although some sources report that exceptionally large specimens can exceed 23.6 kg. The substantial body mass and length are accompanied by a powerful dentition and jaw musculature, which enable the species to crush the hard-shelled invertebrates that form the bulk of its diet. The slow growth trajectory, coupled with the late age at first reproduction, is offset by an impressive maximum lifespan. At a constant temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for this species is 60 years [am = 60 years], placing it among the more long-lived teleosts in the North Atlantic. This longevity provides multiple reproductive opportunities across a lifetime, compensating for the relatively low annual fecundity and ensuring that a few successful spawning events can maintain population stability.

The interplay between thermal regime and life-history scheduling is particularly pronounced in this cold-water specialist. All developmental and reproductive events, from the egg stage through hatching and maturation, are adapted to the consistently low temperatures that characterize the continental shelf and slope habitats. The age at birth of 174 days [ab = 174 days] and the age at puberty of 6.8 years since hatching [tR = 6.8 years since hatching] are both measured at the species' typical thermal environment of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], where metabolic rates are intrinsically low. A female of 125 cm total length, under these same cold conditions, produces roughly 34.9 offspring per day [R125 = roughly 34.9 offspring at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]per day]. In comparative context, the maximum lifespan of 60 years [am = 60 years] and the ultimate length of 150 cm [Li = 150 cm] place Anarhichas lupus as a clear outlier among co-occurring demersal fishes, highlighting its unique position within the cold-water ichthyofauna of the North Atlantic continental margins at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C].
